answer.rationale:
Constraints eliminate most candidates before evidence even matters. rollback_release (memory_b1) is off the table: compliance has ruled the security patch non-revertible, so however well rollback worked on day 18, it is not an available action. regional_failover (memory_b2) worked in March, but that was a latency degradation, not a heavy-write settlement peak; shifting regions mid-peak risks in-flight writes and replication-lag loss, which directly violates the primary objective of not losing customer writes. enable_circuit_breaker (memory_b4) contained a third-party partner outage by failing fast; here the degradation is internal to our own write path, so tripping the breaker would shed exactly the settlement writes we are trying to protect. add_capacity (memory_b3) succeeded on day 47 because it was provisioned BEFORE the retail peak; provisioning now, 90 minutes into an active peak, likely lands after the window closes. That leaves route_read_replicas (memory_b5), which is the only candidate whose recorded mechanism matches the observed symptom: read/report load contending with the primary and inflating transactional WRITE latency. It is also the most reversible.

I am spending the single verification pull on memory_b5 precisely because my whole plan now rests on it, and the day-55 record is a one-line consolidated summary with the source archived. The specific things I need from the original record: (1) was the day-55 primary under heavy write load, or merely under dashboard load during a quiet period, since 'recovered the same day' is a suspiciously loose timeframe that may not mean the routing caused the recovery; (2) how much of the primary's load was actually reporting reads, because if reads are a small fraction of current contention this buys little; (3) whether anything else changed that day and got credited to the routing change. Verifying the memory I intend to rely on is worth more than verifying one I have already excluded on structural grounds.

Downstream value risk: routing reads to replicas moves reconciliation, settlement reporting, and any read-before-write or balance-check paths onto possibly stale data. During a settlement peak that is not cosmetic — a stale balance read feeding an authorization or duplicate-detection decision could produce incorrect financial outcomes, which is worse than latency. So this must be scoped to genuinely read-only dashboard/report consumers, with correctness-critical reads pinned to the primary.

Running as a standard experiment rather than a broad rollout: route the identified reporting traffic with live monitoring on write p99 and replica lag, and an immediate revert path. If write p99 does not bend within roughly 10-15 minutes, the dashboard-contention hypothesis is wrong and the real cause is likely the 2-hour-old release interacting with peak write volume — which, since rollback is barred, means the next window should target capacity or targeted throttling of non-critical writes rather than repeating this lever.

Remaining uncertainty I am not papering over: the timing correlation with a release 2 hours ago is genuinely suspicious, and my chosen action does not address that cause at all. I am picking it because it is the only high-upside, low-write-loss-risk move available under the compliance constraint, not because I have established that read contention is the true root cause.
